text:
Philip Rubin is a pioneering researcher in embodied cognition, particularly in speech and language, with a focus on articulatory synthesis, speech perception, and signal processing. His work at Haskins Laboratories in the 1970s and 1980s laid foundational contributions to speech technology, including the development of ASY (articulatory synthesis) and SWS (sinewave synthesis) systems. Rubin’s innovations, such as speech gestures and the HADES signal processing system, have significantly advanced computational models of speech production and perception.
Throughout his career, Rubin has been deeply involved in science administration, policy, and advocacy. He served as the Director of the Division of Behavioral and Cognitive Sciences at the National Science Foundation (NSF) from 2000 to 2003, and later as a senior advisor in the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP). His leadership roles included chairing the National Academies Board on Behavioral, Cognitive, and Sensory Sciences and serving on various committees addressing ethical issues in research and emerging technologies. Rubin’s theoretical contributions include a dynamical systems/action theory perspective on speech, emphasizing spatiotemporal coordination and the role of embodiment in perception and production. His work also extended to audiovisual speech, multimodality, and the ethical implications of technological advancements.
